title: Trump says Iran called. Qalibaf says Hormuz only under Iranian arrangements. The 90 targets he struck overnight say something else.
narrative:
July 9, 2026 — The US-Iran memorandum of understanding signed June 17, 2026, which imposed a 60-day pause in hostilities and a gradual reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, is in freefall. For the second consecutive night, the US military struck approximately 90 Iranian military targets after Iran attacked three commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on July 8. Iran responded by firing missiles and drones at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, and Jordan.

The public narrative split is stark. President Trump, at the NATO summit in Ankara, told reporters: "To me, it's over. I don't want to deal with them." He also posted on Truth Social: "This is in retribution for yesterday's bombing of ships by Iran. If it happens again, it will get much worse!" Yet on the same flight, Trump told reporters Iran had "called" wanting to make a deal — a claim Iran has not corroborated and which contradicts his own "I don't want to deal with them" formulation.

Iran's position, articulated by chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf: "The Strait of Hormuz will be reopened only under Iranian arrangements, not through US threats." Qatar and Pakistan, the mediating parties, issued statements urging both sides to uphold the MoU — suggesting the mediators themselves were not informed of any "Iran called" outreach.

The three vessels attacked on July 8 — M/T Al Rekayyat, M/T Wedyan, M/T Cyprus Prosperity — were all using routes close to Oman, not Iran's authorised corridor, which Iran cited as a violation of the MoU's spirit. US revocation of the oil-sale license granted under the MoU, announced July 8, further suggests Washington itself treated the agreement as terminated before the vessels were struck.
analysis:
The documentary record shows three contradictory layers that together expose an incoherent US position.

First: Trump's "Iran called" claim vs. Iranian denial. No Iranian official has confirmed any outreach. Qatar's foreign minister called Araghchi on July 9 and condemned Iranian attacks on vessels — not as a warmed-over party to a deal in progress, but as a mediator trying to prevent collapse. The Reuters report of the call, based on the Qatari readout, describes a mediator doing crisis management, not confirming a back-channel.

Second: CENTCOM's "degrading" strikes vs. Iran's successful retaliation. CENTCOM described the strikes as intended to "further degrade" Iran's ability to threaten Hormuz. But Iran successfully struck Patriot systems in Kuwait, an early-warning satellite antenna in Qatar, and a fuel depot in Bahrain — demonstrating the strikes did not degrade Iran's regional reach. The IRGC's claims of these hits have not been confirmed by the target governments, but US officials have not denied them either.

Third: MoU terms vs. "over" declaration. The June 17 MoU was explicit: a 60-day window for technical talks on Hormuz management and Iran's nuclear programme, with the strait to remain open under a specified arrangement. Trump declaring it "over" on July 8 — with 40+ days still remaining — while simultaneously telling reporters "they called" and "I think they're wasting their time" creates an incoherent public position that diplomats cannot operationalize. Qatar and Pakistan, as mediators, issued parallel statements urging adherence to the MoU, implying they had not been informed of any diplomatic off-ramp.

The physical evidence layer: shipping tracking data (Kpler, LSEG) showed zero commercial tanker transits through central Hormuz on July 8-9 despite the MoU's nominal reopening. The three vessels attacked were using Oman-proximate routes, not Iran's authorised corridor — the attribution given by Iran for the strikes. The US revocation of the oil-sale license granted under the MoU, announced the same day as the strikes, is the clearest documentary signal that Washington had already decided to treat the MoU as terminated.
verdict: The load-bearing contradiction is not "who broke the deal" — both sides clearly did — but the simultaneous incoherence in the US position: Trump says the MoU is over, Iran is to blame, Iran called wanting to deal, and the US is winning, all in the same press availability. Iran's response ("not a sign of power, an admission of failure") correctly identifies that a party claiming victory while declaring a negotiation dead does not have a coherent theory of outcome. The CENTCOM footage of destroyed Iranian targets vs. the IRGC footage of Patriot systems in Kuwait burning is the visual evidence of a conflict neither side can claim to be winning or losing — which makes the "Iran called" fabrication the key lie to expose.

documents_in_evidence: Reuters readout of Qatar foreign minister call with Araghchi, July 9, 2026
Qatar/Pakistan joint statement on MoU adherence, July 9, 2026
US revocation of Iran oil-sale license under MoU, July 8, 2026
IRGC statement on Kuwait/Bahrain/Qatar strikes, July 9, 2026
Trump NATO Ankara press availability transcript, July 9, 2026
documents_absent: Any Iranian official confirmation of outreach to US
Any Qatari or Pakistani confirmation of back-channel contact

body:
[SIPHONED VERDICT]: Trump says Iran called to negotiate. Qalibaf says Hormuz only under Iranian arrangements. The 90 targets he struck overnight say something else.

## Narrative

July 9, 2026 — The US-Iran memorandum of understanding signed June 17, 2026, which imposed a 60-day pause in hostilities and a gradual reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, is in freefall. For the second consecutive night, the US military struck approximately 90 Iranian military targets after Iran attacked three commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on July 8. Iran responded by firing missiles and drones at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, and Jordan.

The public narrative split is stark. President Trump, at the NATO summit in Ankara, told reporters: "To me, it's over. I don't want to deal with them." He also posted on Truth Social: "This is in retribution for yesterday's bombing of ships by Iran. If it happens again, it will get much worse!" Yet on the same flight, Trump told reporters Iran had "called" wanting to make a deal — a claim Iran has not corroborated and which contradicts his own "I don't want to deal with them" formulation.

Iran's position, articulated by chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf: "The Strait of Hormuz will be reopened only under Iranian arrangements, not through US threats." Qatar and Pakistan, the mediating parties, issued statements urging both sides to uphold the MoU — suggesting the mediators themselves were not informed of any "Iran called" outreach.

The three vessels attacked on July 8 — M/T Al Rekayyat, M/T Wedyan, M/T Cyprus Prosperity — were all using routes close to Oman, not Iran's authorised corridor, which Iran cited as a violation of the MoU's spirit. US revocation of the oil-sale license granted under the MoU, announced July 8, further suggests Washington itself treated the agreement as terminated before the vessels were struck.

## Analysis

The documentary record shows three contradictory layers that together expose an incoherent US position.

**Trump's "Iran called" claim vs. Iranian denial.** No Iranian official has confirmed any outreach. Qatar's foreign minister called Araghchi on July 9 and condemned Iranian attacks on vessels — not as a warmed-over party to a deal in progress, but as a mediator trying to prevent collapse. The Reuters report of the call, based on the Qatari readout, describes a mediator doing crisis management, not confirming a back-channel.

**CENTCOM's "degrading" strikes vs. Iran's successful retaliation.** CENTCOM described the strikes as intended to "further degrade" Iran's ability to threaten Hormuz. But Iran successfully struck Patriot systems in Kuwait, an early-warning satellite antenna in Qatar, and a fuel depot in Bahrain — demonstrating the strikes did not degrade Iran's regional reach. The IRGC's claims of these hits have not been confirmed by the target governments, but US officials have not denied them either.

**MoU terms vs. "over" declaration.** The June 17 MoU was explicit: a 60-day window for technical talks on Hormuz management and Iran's nuclear programme, with the strait to remain open under a specified arrangement. Trump declaring it "over" on July 8 — with 40+ days still remaining — while simultaneously telling reporters "they called" and "I think they're wasting their time" creates an incoherent public position that diplomats cannot operationalize. Qatar and Pakistan, as mediators, issued parallel statements urging adherence to the MoU, implying they had not been informed of any diplomatic off-ramp.

The physical evidence: shipping tracking data (Kpler, LSEG) showed zero commercial tanker transits through central Hormuz on July 8-9 despite the MoU's nominal reopening. The three vessels attacked were using Oman-proximate routes, not Iran's authorised corridor. The US revocation of the oil-sale license granted under the MoU, announced the same day as the strikes, is the clearest documentary signal that Washington had already decided to treat the MoU as terminated.

## Verdict

The load-bearing contradiction is not "who broke the deal" — both sides clearly did — but the simultaneous incoherence in the US position: Trump says the MoU is over, Iran is to blame, Iran called wanting to deal, and the US is winning, all in the same press availability. Iran's response ("not a sign of power, an admission of failure") correctly identifies that a party claiming victory while declaring a negotiation dead does not have a coherent theory of outcome. The CENTCOM footage of destroyed Iranian targets vs. the IRGC footage of Patriot systems in Kuwait burning is the visual evidence of a conflict neither side can claim to be winning or losing — which makes the "Iran called" fabrication the key lie to expose.
